extracted.intended_audience: math educators, creators of math explanations (YouTube/text/interactive), and math teachers interested in pedagogy and educational content production
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and producing clear, effective mathematical explanations and related educational media (videos, interactive text, games), with advice on pedagogy, sequencing, tooling, and the teacher's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies are a central cognitive tool for mathematicians — 'what is nitrogen for mathematicians, is the analogy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose learners to as many available analogies as possible; analogies help transfer tools/techniques between different areas (e.g., generating functions applied to primes). Conferences and collaborations expand access to useful analogies. Use analogies deliberately to motivate why a concept is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative exposure and travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics progress is highly collaborative; working with others, often by travel or conferences, is important for exposure to new perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek interactions beyond your immediate institution (conferences like MSRI, seminars) to encounter adjacent ideas. For educational creators, collaboration and community feedback can surface new motivating problems and analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start from a motivating problem (motivation for axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good mathematical exposition should explain the motivating problem behind axioms/theory — textbooks often miss this and start with axioms without 'why'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before presenting formalism, show why the axioms/definitions were chosen and what problem they address. Explain historical or applied motivations (e.g., knot theory originating from Lord Kelvin's idea) to justify why a field matters and to cull the vast space of possible formalisms into what’s useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy for the learner's perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense of empathy for possible viewers is essential — knowing what learners need and where they come from shapes good explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contact with real classrooms or intended audiences so you can remember what it’s like not to know something. Losing that empathy (distance in life circumstances) makes explanations less effective. Antipattern: assuming audience knowledge or forgetting novice states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walk learners from not-understanding to understanding (scaffolding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic of a good explanation is 'walking someone on a path from the feeling of not understanding up to the feeling of understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpack concepts incrementally; use concrete examples for initial intuition before abstracting. Explicitly scaffold steps and fill gaps in prerequisite understanding rather than leaping to formal statements. Antipattern: presenting axioms/definitions first without bridging intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt explanations to individual learners
rubrics_metrics.description: The best explanation depends heavily on the individual learner; perfect explanations vary across people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple approaches, analogies, and entry points. Curate resources for different backgrounds. If designing for a broad audience, prioritize generally accessible pathways but consider supplementary targeted explanations for common learner types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive sequencing to induce insight (design of problems/lessons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design content so simple mechanics or initial problems inform progressively harder ones (The Witness example) — sequencing matters for the feeling of epiphany.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order examples/exercises so early tasks teach mechanics that become crucial later; aim for moments where learners 'discover' patterns themselves. Antipattern: random or unconnected problem sets that don't build conceptual momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher role: facilitator, curator, and mentor (beyond motivational speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should do more than motivate: facilitate projects, curate appropriate resources, tailor questions to students' interests, and provide mentorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively select which explanations/resources are best for a given student, propose projects, and give personalized guidance. Antipattern: treating teaching as only inspirational talks without concrete facilitation or follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small instructor interventions matter (sensitivity to initial conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor actions by instructors (a word of encouragement, assigning a problem) can have outsized effects on a student's trajectory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timely encouragement, identify and support promising students, and provide meaningful early research/problem opportunities. Avoid careless negative remarks (antipattern) that can demotivate students on the margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online explanations complement, not replace, in-person teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Top educators publishing online is valuable, but in-person teaching plays unique roles (facilitation, mentorship, maintaining empathy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage experts to produce online content while remaining engaged in classrooms; combine online explanations with in-person mentorship or classroom activities to maximize student development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and production as part of thinking (creator control)
rubrics_metrics.description: For some creators, mundane production/editing details are integral to how they construct the final explanation; editing can be part of the ideation process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that outsourcing editing may impose communication overhead and remove a cognitive tool the creator uses. If outsourcing, document precise intentions and be prepared for iterative back-and-forth. Antipattern: assuming editing is purely mechanical and doesn't influence content decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tooling must support multimodal/visual abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools that only handle text may fail for visuals/animations (Manim example); creators need tooling that understands the desired visual output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose libraries and tooling that align with the visual/animation semantics you need; if using LLM/code assistants, ensure they can represent and modify visual abstractions, or accept that some tasks remain hard to automate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs between reach and depth/time with learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Online reach may be large but individual attention/time is limited; conversely, classroom teaching reaches fewer but can influence students more deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide goals (scale vs depth) and design accordingly: short online explanations for discovery and motivation, deeper in-person or mentored experiences for long-term development. Antipattern: assuming online exposure alone can replicate all roles of in-person teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design explanations for novices with concrete examples and unpacked primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: For audiences without prior context (e.g., societies lacking numeracy), start from concrete examples and deeply unpack primitives like 'what is X?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume shared conceptual frameworks; provide hands-on/counterexample-driven entry points and build vocabulary slowly. Antipattern: starting at an abstraction level that presumes background knowledge.
